title: Science-Fiction Thought Experiments: Real Science Through Invented Worlds
length_note: Eleven classes. Four real subjects need different amounts of room. Epidemiology needs two classes, one on how an outbreak spreads and one on how it is slowed, and logistics needs one more on top of that. Diplomacy and economics each get one class because they use different tools. Linguistics needs two: first what language is, then how people build shared meaning without one. Planetary science needs two: first what makes a world livable, then how and whether to change one. A short opener teaches the method and the 'real vs invented' labelling. A short closing class lets learners apply it. Most classes run 40 minutes, with two shorter ones for the opener and capstone. Each class can be split into two sittings of about 20 minutes, which suits learners who tire easily, such as adults relearning after a brain injury. Every class uses one original invented setting, with no borrowed characters or worlds. Every class ends with a 'Real / Invented / Unknown' ledger, so learners always know which parts are established science and which are story. All sources for facts are to be gathered in the research step, so classes that teach real facts are marked needs_research.

classes.title: What a Thought Experiment Is, and How to Tell Fact from Story
classes.goal: Explain in plain words what a thought experiment is, and sort statements about the course's invented setting into Real, Invented or Unknown.
topics: What a thought experiment is and why scientists and writers use them
Meet the original setting used in every class: a small, invented frontier community with its own people, places and rules
The Real / Invented / Unknown ledger used at the end of every class
Content note: the outbreak classes use an invented, fictional infection, with no gore, and learners can skip any scene

classes.title: Outbreak, Part 1: How an Infection Spreads
classes.goal: Describe how an infection moves through a population and use a simple spreading number to compare two outbreaks.
topics: Real: transmission routes, incubation period, and the basic reproduction number (R0)
Real: why some infections spread faster than others, and what 'exponential growth' looks like
Invented: the story's fictional infection and the 'infected' of the story, shown as a story device with no real-world counterpart
Real vs invented: why real diseases do not behave like movie monsters
Learner activity: change one number in a simple outbreak model and watch what happens

classes.title: Outbreak, Part 2: Slowing It Down
classes.goal: Explain at least three real ways outbreaks are slowed, and say why decisions must be made with incomplete information.
topics: Real: surveillance, testing, contact tracing, isolation and quarantine
Real: vaccines, treatment and hygiene, and how each changes the spreading number
Real: uncertainty in early data and why advice changes as evidence arrives
Fairness and trust: why communities cooperate or do not
Learner activity: advise the invented community with partial information

classes.title: Logistics: Keeping a Community Going
classes.goal: Make a simple supply plan for a small group, covering water, food, power, shelter and medical care, and explain the trade-offs.
topics: Real: the basics of supply chains, stock levels, and single points of failure
Real: water, food, energy and sanitation needs per person, from established humanitarian and emergency-planning guidance
Real: triage and prioritisation as used in emergencies
Invented: the community's map, stores and constraints
Learner activity: build a one-page supply plan and test it against a surprise

classes.title: Diplomacy: The Intergalactic Model UN
classes.goal: Describe how negotiation works between groups with different interests, and take part in a short simulated session.
topics: Real: how model UN and real diplomatic bodies work, including delegations, resolutions, speaking order and voting
Real: interests versus positions, and how compromise and coalitions form
Invented: the delegations of the invented 'Concord of Worlds' and their histories
Learner activity: represent one delegation and draft a short resolution on the shared resource problem from class 4
Optional supports: role cards, sentence starters, and a solo version against scripted delegations

classes.title: Economics: Scarcity, Trade and Fair Shares
classes.goal: Use scarcity, trade and incentives to explain why the Concord's worlds might cooperate or compete, and recognise what a simple model leaves out.
topics: Real: scarcity, opportunity cost, comparative advantage and gains from trade
Real: shared resources, public goods and the 'tragedy of the commons'
Real: sanctions, aid and incentives, and their limits
Invented: the Concord's goods, currencies and distances
Learner activity: set a trade deal between two invented worlds and check who gains and who loses

classes.title: First Contact, Part 1: What Language Is
classes.goal: Name the main parts of any human language and explain why translating an unknown language is hard.
topics: Real: sounds, words, grammar and meaning, and how languages differ
Real: how linguists document an unfamiliar language, including fieldwork methods
Real: why word-for-word translation fails
Invented: the visitors' signals, which are made up for the story and have no real-world counterpart
Real vs unknown: what scientists do and do not know about communication in other animals

classes.title: First Contact, Part 2: Building Shared Meaning
classes.goal: Describe step by step how two groups with no shared language could begin to understand each other, and name the risks of misunderstanding.
topics: Real: pointing and naming, gesture, and how pidgin languages form between groups
Real: how past scripts were deciphered, and the role of bilingual clues
Real: the debate over whether mathematics or physics could serve as a common ground, which is an open question rather than a settled one
Unknown: whether any non-human intelligence exists, and how we would know
Learner activity: decode a short invented signal set using a few clues

classes.title: Terraforming, Part 1: What Makes a World Livable
classes.goal: List the main features that make a planet habitable and compare Earth with at least two other worlds using them.
topics: Real: atmosphere, temperature, liquid water, radiation and magnetic fields
Real: the greenhouse effect and how planets hold or lose heat and air
Real: how Earth, Mars and Venus differ, using measured data
Invented: the story's target world, which is original and not modelled on any existing fictional planet
Learner activity: score the invented world on a habitability checklist

classes.title: Terraforming, Part 2: Methods, Timescales and Ethics
classes.goal: Explain proposed terraforming methods, say which are speculative, and discuss the ethical questions in a balanced way.
topics: Real: proposed methods discussed by scientists, and the limits of what current technology could do
Real: timescales, from decades to millennia, and the energy involved
Real: planetary protection rules and the question of possible native life
Unknown: whether any of these methods would work at full scale
Ethics: who decides, and what is owed to a world and to the people who might one day live there

classes.title: Capstone: Design Your Own Thought Experiment
classes.goal: Create and present a short thought experiment in an original setting, with a Real / Invented / Unknown ledger that is accurate and clear.
topics: Choose one subject from the course: outbreak, logistics, diplomacy, economics, language or planets
Write a one-page scenario with an original setting and no borrowed characters
Build the ledger: label each claim Real, Invented or Unknown, and point to where the real claims came from
Formats on offer: written, spoken, drawn or a short game
Peer feedback and a plain-language self-check
